entries.9938472084c8c459dadcd5e686be5516df6958a2: <div sID="gen11102" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="40" osisID="Ps.40" sID="Ps.40"/> <div eID="gen11102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11103" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11104" type="x-p"/> It should seem David penned this psalm upon occasion of his deliverance, by the power and goodness of God, from some great and pressing trouble, by which he was in danger of being overwhelmed; probably it was some trouble of mind arising from a sense of sin and of God's displeasure against him for it; whatever it was, the same Spirit that indited his praises for that deliverance was in him, at the same time, a Spirit of prophecy, testifying of the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow; or, ere he was aware, he was led to speak of his undertaking, and the discharge of his undertaking, in words that must be applied to Christ only; and therefore how far the praises that here go before that illustrious prophecy, and the prayers that follow, may safely and profitably be applied to him it will be worth while to consider. In this psalm, I. David records God's favour to him in delivering him out of his deep distress, with thankfulness to his praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.40 Ps.1">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Thence he takes occasion to speak of the work of our redemption by Christ, <reference osisRef="Ps.40 Ps.6">ver. 6-10</reference>. III. That gives him encouragement to pray to God for mercy and grace both for himself and for his friends, <reference osisRef="Ps.40 Ps.11">ver. 11-17</reference>. If, in singing this psalm, we mix faith with the prophecy of Christ, and join in sincerity with the praises and prayers here offered up, we make melody with our hearts to the Lord.
entries.ebe298c0d71bb364fa16431d0dc3bb9184714710: <div eID="gen11104" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11103" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Benefit of Confidence in God.</title> <div sID="gen11105" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I waited patiently for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry. 2 He brought me up also out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, <hi type="italic">and</hi> established my goings. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he hath put a new song in my mouth, <hi type="italic">even</hi> praise unto our God: many shall see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and fear, and shall trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 4 Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> that man that maketh the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies. <hi type="super">5</hi> Many, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my God, <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy wonderful works <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou hast done, and thy thoughts <hi type="italic">which are</hi> to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: <hi type="italic">if</hi> I would declare and speak <hi type="italic">of them,</hi> they are more than can be numbered. <div eID="gen11105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11106" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen11106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11107" type="x-p"/> I. The great distress and trouble that the psalmist had been in. He had been plunged into a horrible pit and into miry clay (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.2">v. 2</reference>), out of which he could not work himself, and in which he found himself sinking yet further. He says nothing here either of the sickness of his body or the insults of his enemies, and therefore we have reason to think it was some inward disquiet and perplexity of spirit that was now his greatest grievance. Despondency of spirit under the sense of Gods withdrawings, and prevailing doubts and fears about the eternal state, are indeed a horrible pit and miry clay, and have been so to many a dear child of God. <div eID="gen11107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11108" type="x-p"/> II. His humble attendance upon God and his believing expectations from him in those depths: <hi type="italic">I waited patiently for the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Waiting, I waited.</hi> He expected relief from no other than from God; the same hand that tears must heal, that smites must bind up (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Hos. vi. 1</reference>), or it will never be done. From God he expected relief, and he was big with expectation, not doubting but it would come in due time. There is power enough in God to help the weakest, and grace enough in God to help the unworthiest, of all his people that trust in him. But he waited patiently, which intimates that the relief did not come quickly; yet he doubted not but it would come, and resolved to continue believing, and hoping, and praying, till it did come. Those whose expectation is from God may wait with assurance, but must wait with patience. Now this is very applicable to Christ. His agony, both in the garden and on the cross, was the same continued, and it was a horrible pit and miry clay. Then was his soul troubled and exceedingly sorrowful; but then he prayed, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name; Father, save me;</hi> then he kept hold of his relation to his Father, "My God, my God," and thus waited patiently for him. <div eID="gen11108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11109" type="x-p"/> III. His comfortable experience of God's goodness to him in his distress, which he records for the honour of God and his own and others' encouragement. <div eID="gen11109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11110" type="x-p"/> 1. God answered his prayers: <hi type="italic">He inclined unto me and heard my cry.</hi> Those that wait patiently for God, though they may wait long, do not wait in vain. Our Lord Jesus was <hi type="italic">heard in that he feared,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. Nay, he was sure that the Father heard him always. <div eID="gen11110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11111" type="x-p"/> 2. He silenced his fears, and stilled the tumult of his spirits, and gave him a settled peace of conscience (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.2">v. 2</reference>): "He <hi type="italic">brought me up out of that horrible pit</hi> of despondency and despair, scattered the clouds, and shone brightly upon my soul, with the assurances of his favour; and not only so, but <hi type="italic">set my feet upon a rock and established my goings.</hi>" Those that have been under the prevalency of a religious melancholy, and by the grace of God have been relieved, may apply this very feelingly to themselves; they are brought up out of a horrible pit. (1.) The mercy is completed by the setting of their feet upon a rock, where they find firm footing, are as much elevated with the hopes of heaven as they were before cast down with the fears of hell. Christ is the rock on which a poor soul may stand fast, and on whose meditation alone between us and God we can build any solid hopes or satisfaction. (2.) It is continued in the establishment of their goings. Where God has given a stedfast hope he expects there should be a steady regular conversation; and, if that be the blessed fruit of it, we have reason to acknowledge, with abundance of thankfulness, the riches and power of his grace. <div eID="gen11111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11112" type="x-p"/> 3. He filled him with joy, as well as peace, in believing: "<hi type="italic">He has put a new song in my mouth;</hi> he has given me cause to rejoice and a heart to rejoice." He was brought, as it were, into a new world, and that filled his mouth with a new song, <hi type="italic">even praise to our God;</hi> for to his praise and glory must all our songs be sung. Fresh mercies, especially such as we never before received, call for new songs. This is applicable to our Lord Jesus in his reception to paradise, his resurrection from the grave, and his exaltation to the joy and glory set before him; he was brought out of the horrible pit, set upon a rock, and had a new song put into his mouth. <div eID="gen11112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11113" type="x-p"/> IV. The good improvement that should be made of this instance of God's goodness to David. <div eID="gen11113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11114" type="x-p"/> 1. David's experience would be an encouragement to many to hope in God, and, for that end, he leaves it here upon record: <hi type="italic">Many shall see, and fear, and trust in the Lord.</hi> They shall fear the Lord and his justice, which brought David, and the Son of David, into that horrible pit, and shall say, <hi type="italic">If this be done to the green tree, what shall be done to the dry?</hi> They shall fear the Lord and his goodness, in filling the mouth of David, and the Son of David, with new songs of joy and praise. There is a holy reverent fear of God, which is not only consistent with, but the foundation of, our hope in him. They shall not fear him and shun him, but fear him and trust in him in their greatest straits, not doubting but to find him as able and ready to help as David did in his distress. God's dealings with our Lord Jesus are our great encouragement to trust in God; when it pleased the Lord to bruise him, and put him to grief for our sins, he demanded our debt from him; and when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand, he made it to appear that he had accepted the payment he made and was satisfied with it; and what greater encouragement can we have to fear and worship God and to<hi type="italic">trust in him?.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Rom. iv. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1-Rom.5.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. The psalmist invites others to make God their hope, as he did, by pronouncing those happy that do so (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Blessed is the man that makes the Lord his trust,</hi> and him only (that has great and good thoughts of him, and is entirely devoted to him), <hi type="italic">and respects not the proud,</hi> does not do as those do that trust in themselves, nor depends upon those who proudly encourage others to trust in them; for both the one and the other turn aside to lies, as indeed all those do that turn aside from God." This is applicable, particularly, to our faith in Christ. Blessed are those that trust in him, and in his righteousness alone, and respect not the proud Pharisees, that set up their own righteousness in competition with that, that will not be governed by their dictates, nor turn aside to lies, with the unbelieving Jews, who <hi type="italic">submit not to the righteousness of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Rom. x. 3</reference>. Blessed are those that escape this temptation. <div eID="gen11114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11115" type="x-p"/> 2. The joyful sense he had of this mercy led him to observe, with thankfulness, the many other favours he had received from God, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">v. 5</reference>. When God puts new songs into our mouth we must not forget our former songs, but repeat them: "<hi type="italic">Many, O Lord my God! are thy wonderful works which thou hast done,</hi> both for me and others; this is but one of many." Many are the benefits with which we are daily loaded both by the providence and by the grace of God. (1.) They are his works, not only the gifts of his bounty, but the operations of his power. He works for us, he works in us, and thus he favours us with matter, not only for thanks, but for praise. (2.) They are his wonderful works, the contrivance of them admirable, his condescension to us in bestowing them upon us admirable; eternity itself will be short enough to be spent in the admiration of them. (3.) All his wonderful works are the product of his thoughts to us-ward. He does all <hi type="italic">according to the counsel of his own will</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Eph. i. 11</reference>), the purposes of his grace <hi type="italic">which he purposed in himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.11">Eph. iii. 11</reference>. They are the projects of infinite wisdom, the designs of everlasting love (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1 Cor. ii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer. xxxi. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">thoughts of good and not of evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">Jer. xxix. 11</reference>. His gifts and callings will <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> be without repentance, because they are not sudden resolves, but the result of his thoughts, his many thoughts, to us-ward. (4.) They are innumerable; they cannot be methodized or <hi type="italic">reckoned up in order.</hi> There is an order in all God's works, but there are so many that present themselves to our view at once that we know not where to begin nor which to name next; the order of them, and their natural references and dependencies, and how the links of the golden chain are joined, are a mystery to us, and what we shall not be able to account for till the veil be rent and the mystery of God finished. Nor can they be counted, not the very heads of them. When we have said the most we can of the wonders of divine love to us we must conclude with an <hi type="italic">et cætera—and such like,</hi> and adore the depth, despairing to find the bottom.
entries.c8d6a000cf73a6adf96356e700127608210dc068: <div eID="gen11115" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Insufficiency of the Legal Sacrifices; The Efficacy of Christ's Sacrifice.</title> <div sID="gen11116" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written of me, <hi type="super">8</hi> I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law <hi type="italic">is</hi> within my heart. <hi type="super">9</hi> I have preached righteousness in the great congregation: lo, I have not refrained my lips, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thou knowest. <hi type="super">10</hi> I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation. <div eID="gen11116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11117" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, being struck with amazement at the wonderful works that God had done for his people, is strangely carried out here to foretel that work of wonder which excels all the rest and is the foundation and fountain of all, that of our redemption by our Lord Jesus Christ. God's thoughts, which were to us-ward concerning that work, were the most curious, the most copious, the most gracious, and therefore to be most admired. This paragraph is quoted by the apostle (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.5-Heb.10.7">Heb. x. 5</reference>, &c.) and applied to Christ and his undertaking for us. As in the institutions, so in the devotions, of the Old Testament saints were aware of; and, when the apostle would show us the Redeemer's voluntary undertaking of his work, he does not fetch his account out of the book of God's secret counsels, which belong not to us, but from the things revealed. Observe, <div eID="gen11117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11118" type="x-p"/> I. The utter insufficiency of the legal sacrifices to atone for sin in order to our peace with God and our happiness in him: <hi type="italic">Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire;</hi> thou wouldst not have the Redeemer to offer them. Something he must have to offer, but not these (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.3">Heb. viii. 3</reference>); therefore he must not be of the house of Aaron, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.14">Heb. vii. 14</reference>. Or, In the days of the Messiah burnt-offering and sin-offering will be no longer required, but all those ceremonial institutions will be abolished. But that is not all: even while the law concerning them was in full force it might be said, God did not desire them, nor accept them, for their own sake. They could not take away the guilt of sin by satisfying God's justice. The life of a sheep, which is so much inferior in value to that of a man (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.12">Matt. xii. 12</reference>), could not pretend to be an equivalent, much less an expedient to preserve the honour of God's government and laws and repair the injury done to that honour by the sin of man. They could not take away the terror of sin by pacifying the conscience, nor the power of sin by sanctifying the nature; it was impossible, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.9">Heb. ix. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="10.1-4">x. 1-4</reference>. What there was in them that was valuable resulted from their reference to Jesus Christ, of whom they were types—shadows indeed, but shadows of good things to come, and trials of the faith and obedience of God's people, of their obedience to the law, and their faith in the gospel. But the Substance must come, which is Christ, who must bring that glory to God, and that grace to man which it was impossible those sacrifices should ever do. <div eID="gen11118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11119" type="x-p"/> II. The designation of our Lord Jesus to the work and office of Mediator: <hi type="italic">My ears hast thou opened.</hi> God the Father disposed him to the undertaking (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.5-Isa.50.6">Isa. l. 5, 6</reference>) and then obliged him to go through with it. <hi type="italic">My ear hast thou digged.</hi> It is supposed to allude to the law and custom of binding servants to serve for ever by boring their ear to the doorpost; see <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exod. xxi. 6</reference>. Our Lord Jesus was so in love with his undertaking that he would not go out free from it, and therefore engaged to persevere for ever in it; and for this reason <hi type="italic">he is able to save us to the uttermost,</hi> because he has engaged to serve his Father to the uttermost, who upholds him in it, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen11119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11120" type="x-p"/> III. His own voluntary consent to this undertaking: "<hi type="italic">Then said I, Lo, I come;</hi> then, when sacrifice and offering would not do, rather than the work should be undone; I said, Lo, I come, to enter the lists with the powers of darkness, and to advance the interests of God's glory and kingdom." This intimates three things:—1. That he freely offered himself to this service, to which he was under no obligation at all prior to his own voluntary engagement. It was no sooner proposed to him than, with the greatest cheerfulness, he consented to it, and was wonderfully well pleased with the undertaking. Had he not been perfectly voluntary in it, he could not have been a surety, he could not have been a sacrifice; for it is by this will (this <hi type="italic">animus offerentis—mind of the offerer</hi>) that we are sanctified, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.10">Heb. x. 10</reference>. 2. That he firmly obliged himself to it: "I come; I promise to come in the fulness of time." And therefore the apostle says, "It was when he came into the world that he had an actual regard to this promise, by which he had <hi type="italic">engaged his heart to approach unto God.</hi>" He thus entered into bonds, not only to show the greatness of his love, but because he was to have the honour of his undertaking before he had fully performed it. Though the price was not paid, it was secured to be paid, so that he was the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. 3. That he frankly owned himself engaged: He said, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come,</hi> said it all along to the Old Testament saints, who therefore knew him by the title of <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho erchomenos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He that should come.</hi> This word was the foundation on which they built their faith and hope, and which they looked and longed for the accomplishment of. <div eID="gen11120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11121" type="x-p"/> IV. The reason why he came, in pursuance of his undertaking—because <hi type="italic">in the volume of the book it was written of him,</hi> 1. In the close rolls of the divine decree and counsel; there it was written that his ear was opened, and he said, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come;</hi> there the covenant of redemption was recorded, the counsel of redemption was recorded, the counsel of peace between the Father and the Son; and to that he had an eye in all he did, the commandment he received of his Father. 2. In the letters patent of the Old Testament. Moses and all the prophets testified of him; in all the volumes of that book something or other was written of him, which he had an eye to, that all might be accomplished, <reference osisRef="John.19.28">John xix. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen11121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11122" type="x-p"/> V. The pleasure he took in his undertaking. Having freely offered himself to it, he did not fail, nor was discouraged, but proceeded with all possible satisfaction to himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.8-Ps.40.9">v. 8, 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I delight to do thy will, O my God!</hi> It was to Christ his meat and drink to go on with the work appointed to him (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">John iv. 34</reference>); and the reason here given is, <hi type="italic">Thy law is within my heart;</hi> it is written there, it rules there. It is meant of the law concerning the work and office of the Mediator, what he was to do and suffer; this law was dear to him and had an influence upon him in his whole undertaking. Note, When the law of God is written in our hearts our duty will be our delight. <div eID="gen11122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11123" type="x-p"/> VI. The publication of the gospel to the children of men, even <hi type="italic">in the great congregation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.9-Ps.40.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. The same that as a priest wrought out redemption for us, as a prophet, by his own preaching first, then by his apostles, and still by his word and Spirit, makes it known to us. The <hi type="italic">great salvation began to be spoken by the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.3">Heb. ii. 3</reference>. It is the gospel of Christ that is preached to all nations. Observe, 1. What it is that is preached: It is <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.9">v. 9</reference>), God's righteousness (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">v. 10</reference>), the everlasting righteousness which Christ has brought in (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>); compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16-Rom.1.17">Rom. i. 16, 17</reference>. It is God's <hi type="italic">faithfulness</hi> to his promise, and the salvation which had long been looked for. It is God's <hi type="italic">lovingkindness</hi> and his <hi type="italic">truth,</hi> his mercy according to his word. Note, In the work of our redemption we ought to take notice how brightly all the divine attributions shine, and give to God the praise of each of them. 2. To whom it is preached—<hi type="italic">to the great congregation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.9">v. 9</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">v. 10</reference>. When Christ was here on earth he preached to multitudes, thousands at a time. The gospel was preached both to Jews and Gentiles, to great congregations of both. Solemn religious assemblies are a divine institution, and in them the glory of God, in the face of Christ, ought to be both praised to the glory of God and preached for the edification of men. 3. How it is preached—freely and openly: <hi type="italic">I have not refrained my lips; I have not hid it; I have not concealed it.</hi> This intimates that whoever undertook to preach the gospel of Christ would be in great temptation to hide it and conceal it, because it must be preached with great contention and in the face of great opposition; but Christ himself, and those whom he called to that work, set their faces <hi type="italic">as a flint</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa. l. 7</reference>) and were wonderfully carried on in it. It is well for us that they were so, for by this means our eyes come to see this joyful light and our ears to hear this joyful sound, which otherwise we might for ever have perished in ignorance of.
entries.2017628c0de02912938ee0b63aa8687abad6d417: <div eID="gen11123" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement in Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen11124" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Withhold not thou thy tender mercies from me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : let thy lovingkindness and thy truth continually preserve me. <hi type="super">12</hi> For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me. <hi type="super">13</hi> Be pleased, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , to deliver me: <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , make haste to help me. <hi type="super">14</hi> Let them be ashamed and confounded together that seek after my soul to destroy it; let them be driven backward and put to shame that wish me evil. <hi type="super">15</hi> Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha. <hi type="super">16</hi> Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: let such as love thy salvation say continually, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be magnified. 17 But I <hi type="italic">am</hi> poor and needy; <hi type="italic">yet</hi> the Lord thinketh upon me: thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God. <div eID="gen11124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11125" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having meditated upon the work of redemption, and spoken of it in the person of the Messiah, now comes to make improvement of the doctrine of his mediation between us and God, and therefore speaks in his own person. Christ having done his Father's will, and finished his work, and given orders for the preaching of the gospel to every creature, we are encouraged to come boldly to the throne of grace, for mercy and grace. <div eID="gen11125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11126" type="x-p"/> I. This may encourage us to pray for the mercy of God, and to put ourselves under the protection of that mercy, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.11">v. 11</reference>. "Lord, thou hast not spared thy Son, nor withheld him; <hi type="italic">withhold not thou thy tender mercies</hi> then, which thou hast laid up for us in him; for wilt thou not <hi type="italic">with him also freely give us all things?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.32">Rom. viii. 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">Let thy lovingkindness and thy truth continually preserve me.</hi>" The best saints are in continual danger, and see themselves undone if they be not continually preserved by the grace of God; and the everlasting lovingkindness and truth of God are what we have to depend upon for our preservation to the heavenly kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.7">Ps. lxi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen11126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11127" type="x-p"/> II. This may encourage us in reference to the guilt of sin, that Jesus Christ has done that towards our discharge from it which sacrifice and offering could not do. See here, 1. The frightful sight he had of sin, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">v. 12</reference>. This was it that made the discovery he was now favoured with of a Redeemer very welcome to him. He saw his iniquities to be evils, the worst of evils; he saw that they <hi type="italic">compassed him about;</hi> in all the reviews of his life, and his reflections upon each step of it, still he discovered something amiss. The threatening consequences of his sin surrounded him. Look which way he would, he saw some mischief or other waiting for him, which he was conscious to himself his sins had deserved. He saw them taking hold of him, arresting him, as the bailiff does the poor debtor; he saw them to be innumerable and <hi type="italic">more than the hairs of his head.</hi> Convinced awakened consciences are apprehensive of danger from the numberless number of the sins of infirmity which seem small as hairs, but, being numerous, are very dangerous. <hi type="italic">Who can understand his errors?</hi> God numbers our hairs (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.30">Matt. x. 30</reference>), which yet we cannot number; so he keeps an account of our sins, which we keep no account of. The sight of sin so oppressed him that he could not hold up his head—<hi type="italic">I am not able to look up;</hi> much less could he keep up his heart—<hi type="italic">therefore my heart fails me.</hi> Note, The sight of our sins in their own colours would drive us to distraction, if we had not at the same time some sight of a Saviour. 2. The careful recourse he had to God under the sense of sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.13">v. 13</reference>); seeing himself brought by his sins to the very brink of ruin, eternal ruin, with what a holy passion does he cry out, "<hi type="italic">Be pleased, O Lord! to deliver me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.13">v. 13</reference>); O save me from the wrath to come, and the present terrors I am in through the apprehensions of that wrath! I am undone, I die, I perish, without speedy relief. In a case of this nature, where the bliss of an immortal soul is concerned, delays are dangerous; therefore, <hi type="italic">O Lord! make haste to help me.</hi>" <div eID="gen11127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11128" type="x-p"/> III. This may encourage us to hope for victory over our spiritual enemies that seek after our souls to destroy them (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.14">v. 14</reference>), the roaring lion that goes about continually seeking to devour. If Christ has triumphed over them, we through him, shall be more than conquerors. In the belief of this we may pray, with humble boldness, <hi type="italic">Let them be ashamed and confounded together,</hi> and <hi type="italic">driven backward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Let them be desolate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.15">v. 15</reference>. Both the conversion of a sinner and the glorification of a saint are great disappointments to Satan, who does his utmost, with all his power and subtlety, to hinder both. Now, our Lord Jesus having undertaken to bring about the salvation of all his chosen, we may in faith pray that, in both these ways, that great adversary may be confounded. When a child of God is brought into that horrible pit, and the miry clay, Satan cries <hi type="italic">Aha! aha!</hi> thinking he has gained his point; but he shall rage when he sees the brand plucked out of the fire, and shall be <hi type="italic">desolate, for a reward of his shame. The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan! The accuser of the brethren is cast out.</hi> <div eID="gen11128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11129" type="x-p"/> IV. This may encourage all that seek God, and love his salvation, to rejoice in him and to praise him, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.16">v. 16</reference>. See here, 1. The character of good people. Conformably to the laws of natural religion, they seek God, desire his favour, and in all their exigencies apply to him, as a people should seek unto their God; and conformably to the laws of revealed religion they <hi type="italic">love his salvation,</hi> that great salvation of which the prophets enquired and searched diligently, which the Redeemer undertook to work out when he said, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come.</hi> All that shall be saved love the salvation not only as a salvation from hell, but a salvation from sin. 2. The happiness secured to good people by this prophetic prayer. Those that seek God shall <hi type="italic">rejoice and be glad in him,</hi> and with good reason, for he will not only be found of them but will be their bountiful rewarder. Those that love his salvation shall be filled with the joy of his salvation, and shall <hi type="italic">say continually, The Lord be magnified;</hi> and thus they shall have a heaven upon earth. Blessed are those that are thus still praising God. <div eID="gen11129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11130" type="x-p"/> V. This may encourage the saints, in distress and affliction, to trust in God and comfort themselves in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.17">v. 17</reference>. David himself was one of these: <hi type="italic">I am poor and needy</hi> (a king, perhaps now on the throne, and yet, being troubled in spirit, he calls himself <hi type="italic">poor and needy,</hi> in want and distress, lost and undone without a Saviour), <hi type="italic">yet the Lord thinketh upon me</hi> in and through the Mediator, by whom we are made accepted. Men forget the poor and needy, and seldom think of them; but God's thoughts, towards them (which he had spoken of <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">v. 5</reference>) are their support and comfort. They may assure themselves that God is their help under their troubles, and will be, in due time, their deliverer out of their troubles, and will make no long tarrying; for <hi type="italic">the vision is for an appointed time,</hi> and therefore, <hi type="italic">though it tarry,</hi> we may <hi type="italic">wait for it,</hi> for it shall come; <hi type="italic">it will come, it will not tarry.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.40"/> <div eID="gen11130" type="x-p"/>

entries.5e2fca41517f41fb4fa7b0e93e426651665fda88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5925"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 40</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.40.1-Ps.40.17">Psa 40:1-17</reference>. In this Psalm a celebration of God's deliverance is followed by a profession of devotion to His service. Then follows a prayer for relief from imminent dangers, involving the overthrow of enemies and the rejoicing of sympathizing friends. In <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>, &c., Paul quotes <reference osisRef="Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8">Psa 40:6-8</reference> as the words of Christ, offering Himself as a better sacrifice. Some suppose Paul thus accommodated David's words to express Christ's sentiments. But the value of his quotation would be thus destroyed, as it would have no force in his argument, unless regarded by his readers as the original sense of the passage in the Old Testament. Others suppose the Psalm describes David's feelings in suffering and joy; but the language quoted by Paul, in the sense given by him, could not apply to David in any of his relations, for as a type the language is not adapted to describe any event or condition of David's career, and as an individual representing the pious generally, neither he nor they could properly use it (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference>, below). The Psalm must be taken then, as the sixteenth, to express the feelings of Christ's human nature. The difficulties pertinent to this view will be considered as they occur.</title> <div sID="gen9009" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5925"/>1-3. The figures for deep distress are illustrated in Jeremiah's history (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.6-Jer.38.12">Jr 38:6-12</reference>). Patience and trust manifested in distress, deliverance in answer to prayer, and the blessed effect of it in eliciting praise from God's true worshippers, teach us that Christ's suffering is our example, and His deliverance our encouragement (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">He 5:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.3">12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.12-1Pet.4.16">1Pe 4:12-16</reference>).<div eID="gen9009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inclined--</hi>(the ear, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">Psa 17:6</reference>), as if to catch the faintest sigh. <div eID="gen9010" type="x-p"/>
entries.40e14b73358c2b36a3776c6544360d84784d2c25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5927"/><div sID="gen9013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5927"/><hi type="bold">4. Blessed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>; 2:12).<div eID="gen9013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">respecteth--</hi>literally, "turns towards," as an object of confidence.<div eID="gen9014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn aside--</hi>from true God and His law to falsehood in worship and conduct. <div eID="gen9015" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7f9d94b1ad37c1cae6ee923ffc40a9ac4d78b7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5928"/><div sID="gen9016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5928"/><hi type="bold">5. be reckoned up in order--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.3">Psa 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.14">33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">Is 44:7</reference>), too many to be set forth regularly. This is but one instance of many. The use of the plural accords with the union of Christ and His people. In suffering and triumph, they are one with Him. <div eID="gen9016" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a7fbf2d39548b8c7eccabe14de00f2327892e5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5929"/><div sID="gen9017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5929"/>6-8. In Paul's view this passage has more meaning than the mere expression of grateful devotion to God's service. He represents Christ as declaring that the sacrifices, whether vegetable or animal, general or special expiatory offerings, would not avail to meet the demands of God's law, and that He had come to render the required satisfaction, which he states was effected by "the offering of the body of Christ" [He 10:10], for that is the "will of God" which Christ came to fulfil or do, in order to effect man's redemption. We thus see that the contrast to the unsatisfactory character assigned the Old Testament offerings in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference> is found in the compliance with God's law (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">8</reference>). Of course, as Paul and other New Testament writers explain Christ's work, it consisted in more than being made under the law or obeying its precepts. It required an "obedience unto death" [Php 2:8], and that is the compliance here chiefly intended, and which makes the contrast with <reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference> clear.<div eID="gen9017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine ears hast thou opened--</hi>Whether allusion is made to the custom of boring a servant's ear, in token of voluntary and perpetual enslavement (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Ex 21:6</reference>), or that the opening of the ear, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Is 48:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.5">50:5</reference> (though by a different word in Hebrew) denotes obedience by the common figure of hearing for obeying, it is evident that the clause is designed to express a devotion to God's will as avowed more fully in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">Psa 40:8</reference>, and already explained. Paul, however, uses the words, "a body hast thou prepared me" [He 10:5], which are found in the Septuagint in the place of the words, "mine ears hast thou opened." He does not lay any stress on this clause, and his argument is complete without it. It is, perhaps, to be regarded rather as an interpretation or free translation by the Septuagint, than either an addition or attempt at verbal translation. The Septuagint translators may have had reference to Christ's vicarious sufferings as taught in other Scriptures, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4-Isa.53.11">Is 53:4-11</reference>; at all events, the sense is substantially the same, as a body was essential to the required obedience (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">Ro 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>). <div eID="gen9018" type="x-p"/>
entries.576796cff7955b7fac76ea0a202793af2ddf1c6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5931"/><div sID="gen9023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5931"/><hi type="bold">9-10. I have preached--</hi>literally, "announced good tidings." Christ's prophetical office is taught. He "preached" the great truths of God's government of sinners. <div eID="gen9023" type="x-p"/>
entries.74e97689c66cae8448cbb5279899323872b49805: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5932"/><div sID="gen9024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5932"/>11. may be rendered as an assertion, that God will not withhold (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>). <div eID="gen9024" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c7ef77f9a82d92919f439f435091dc59f52fda9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5933"/><div sID="gen9025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5933"/><hi type="bold">12. evils--</hi>inflicted by others.<div eID="gen9025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquities--</hi>or penal afflictions, and sometimes calamities in the wide sense. This meaning of the word is very common (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.11">Psa 31:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.4">38:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.4.13">Ge 4:13</reference>, Cain's punishment; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.15">Ge 19:15</reference>, that of Sodom; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.10">1Sa 28:10</reference>, of the witch of En-dor; also <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.12">2Sa 16:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.29">Job 19:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.18">Is 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">53:11</reference>). This meaning of the word is also favored by the clause, "taken hold of me," which follows, which can be said appropriately of sufferings, but not of sins (compare <reference osisRef="Job.27.20">Job 27:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.24">Psa 69:24</reference>). Thus, the difficulties in referring this Psalm to Christ, arising from the usual reading of this verse, are removed. Of the terrible afflictions, or sufferings, alluded to and endured for us, compare <reference osisRef="Luke.22.39-Luke.22.44">Lu 22:39-44</reference>, and the narrative of the scenes of Calvary.<div eID="gen9026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my heart faileth me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.26.38">Mt 26:38</reference>), "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death."<div eID="gen9027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot look up--</hi>literally, "I cannot see," not denoting the depression of conscious guilt, as <reference osisRef="Luke.18.13">Lu 18:13</reference>, but exhaustion from suffering, as dimness of eyes (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.10">38:10</reference>). The whole context thus sustains the sense assigned to iniquities. <div eID="gen9028" type="x-p"/>
entries.4282e19e6e07de583b8cfab0bb384e0a791446b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5934"/><div sID="gen9029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5934"/>13. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.19">Psa 22:19</reference>). <div eID="gen9029" type="x-p"/>
entries.330e7aa2e10d848ffec187de73877eb45fd919e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5935"/><div sID="gen9030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5935"/>14-15. The language is not necessarily imprecatory, but rather a confident expectation (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.11">Psa 5:11</reference>), though the former sense is not inconsistent with Christ's prayer for the forgiveness of His murderers, inasmuch as their confusion and shame might be the very means to prepare them for humbly seeking forgiveness (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.37">Ac 2:37</reference>). <div eID="gen9030" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff51ab792d1021be9e39db047eedf802a5c30ac3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5937"/><div sID="gen9033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5937"/>16. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.35.27">Psa 35:27</reference>).<div eID="gen9033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love thy salvation--</hi>delight in its bestowal on others as well as themselves. <div eID="gen9034" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbe118b4097d39c74e6973e9322a990d58f1cde7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5938"/><div sID="gen9035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5938"/>17. A summary of his condition and hopes.<div eID="gen9035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thinketh upon--</hi>or provides for me. "He was heard," "when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, unto Him that was able to save him from death" [He 5:7]. <chapter eID="Ps.40"/>

entries.53a25e4810496575c3378073002e048c5227f288: <div eID="gen19900" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19901" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19902" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19902" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19901" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19903" type="x-p"/> The benefit of confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.1-Psa.40.3">Psa 40:1-3</reference>. The blessedness of those who trust in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.5">Psa 40:5</reference>. The termination of the Jewish sacrifices in that of Christ, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.6-Psa.40.8">Psa 40:6-8</reference>. The psalmist's resolution to publish God's goodness, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.9">Psa 40:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.10">Psa 40:10</reference> : he prays to be delivered from evils, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.11-Psa.40.13">Psa 40:11-13</reference>; against his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.14">Psa 40:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.15">Psa 40:15</reference>; and in behalf of those who are destitute, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.16">Psa 40:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.17">Psa 40:17</reference>. <div eID="gen19903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19904" type="x-p"/> The Title, "To the chief Musician," we have already seen, and it contains nothing worthy of particular remark. Concerning the occasion and author of this Psalm there has been a strange and numerous diversity of opinions. I shall not trouble the reader with sentiments which I believe to be ill founded; as I am satisfied the Psalm was composed by David and about the same time and on the same occasion as the two preceding; with this difference, that here he magnifies God for having bestowed the mercy which he sought there. It is, therefore, a thanksgiving for his recovery from the sore disease by which he was afflicted in his body, and for his restoration to the Divine favor. The sixth, seventh, and eighth verses contain a remarkable prophecy of the incarnation and sacrificial offering of Jesus Christ. From the eleventh to the end contains a new subject and appears to have belonged to another Psalm. It is the same as the seventieth Psalm; only it wants the two first verses. <div eID="gen19904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19905" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19906" type="x-p"/> I waited patiently for the Lord - The two preceding Psalms are proofs of the patience and resignation with which David waited for the mercy of God. The reader is requested to consult the notes on them. <div eID="gen19906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19907" type="x-p"/> And heard my cry - The two preceding Psalms show how he prayed and waited; this shows how he succeeded.
entries.726a26fb0d918cac16d6b18a73117d3b8f86831c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19908" type="x-p"/> A horrible pit - Literally, the sounding pit; where nothing was heard except the howlings of wild beasts, or the hollow sounds of winds reverberated and broken from the craggy sides and roof. <div eID="gen19908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19909" type="x-p"/> The miry clay - Where the longer I stayed the deeper I sank, and was utterly unable to save myself. The Syriac and Arabic translate "The pit of perdition, and the mud of corruption." These are figurative expressions to point out the dreary, dismal, ruinous state of sin and guilt, and the utter inability of a condemned sinner to save himself either from the guilt of his conscience, or the corruption of his heart. <div eID="gen19909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19910" type="x-p"/> Set my feet upon a rock - Thou hast changed my state from guilt to pardon; from corruption to holiness; in consequence of which my goings are established. I have now power over all sin, and can walk steadily in the way that leads to God's kingdom.
entries.9a8947cee06fc743b29ab5c600d94f6ebc23b335: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19911" type="x-p"/> A new song - Cheerfulness and joy had long been strangers to him. He seemed to live to utter the most doleful complaints, and be a prey to suffering and wretchedness. Praise for a sense of God's favor was a new song to him. The word is often used to signify excellence: I will sing a most excellent and eminent song. <div eID="gen19911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19912" type="x-p"/> Many shalt see it - I will publish it abroad and fear-to sin against the Lord, knowing by my example what a grievous and bitter thing it is. <div eID="gen19912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19913" type="x-p"/> And shall trust in the Lord - Even the worst of sinners shall not despair of mercy, being penitent, when they see that I have found favor in his sight.
entries.dd587cf791ee6680336d8141dc723f4b440e1e57: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19914" type="x-p"/> Blessed is that man - The man must be blessed and happy who casts his soul with all its burden of sin and wretchedness, at the footstool of God's mercy; for he will save all who come to him through the Son of his love.
entries.a8c6ffe4896c7fd7bbe624a3141070b4c30f2952: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19915" type="x-p"/> Many - are thy wonderful works - The psalmist seems here astonished and confounded at the counsels, loving-kindnesses, and marvellous works of the Lord, not in nature, but in grace; for it was the mercy of God towards himself that he had now particularly in view.
entries.49be463182b930bc60b314b20f14b6184c93fdbe: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19916" type="x-p"/> Sacrifice and offering - The apostle, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">Heb 10:5</reference>, etc., quoting this and the two following verses, says, When he (the Messiah) cometh into the world - was about to be incarnated, He saith - to God the Father, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldst not - it was never thy will and design that the sacrifices under thy own law should be considered as making atonement for sin; they were only designed to point out my incarnation and consequent sacrificial death: and therefore a body hast thou prepared me, by a miraculous conception in the womb of a virgin; according to thy word, The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent. <div eID="gen19916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19917" type="x-p"/> A body hast thou prepared me - The quotation of this and the two following verses by the apostle, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">Heb 10:5</reference>, etc., is taken from the Septuagint, with scarcely any variety of reading: but, although the general meaning is the same, they are widely different in verbal expression in the Hebrew. David's words are אזנים כרית לי oznayim caritha lli, which we translate, My ears hast thou opened; but they might be more properly rendered, My ears hast thou bored; that is, Thou hast made me thy servant for ever, to dwell in thine own house: for the allusion is evidently to the custom mentioned <reference osisRef="Exo.21.2">Exo 21:2</reference>, etc.: "If thou buy a Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free: but if the servant shall positively say, I love my master, etc., I will not go out free; then his master shall bring him to the doorpost, and shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall serve him for ever." <div eID="gen19917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19918" type="x-p"/> But how is it possible that the Septuagint and the apostle should take a meaning so totally different from the sense of the Hebrew? Dr. Kennicott has a very ingenious conjecture here: he supposes that the Septuagint and apostle express the meaning of the words as they stood in the copy from which the Greek translation was made; and that the present Hebrew text is corrupted in the word אזנים oznayim, ears, which has been written through carelessness for אז גוה az gevah, Then, a Body The first syllable, אז az, Then, is the same in both; and the latter, Myn, which, joined to אז makes אזנים oznayim, might have been easily mistaken for גוה gevah, Body; נ nun being very like ג gimel; י yod like ו vau; and h he like final ם mem; especially if the line on which the letters were written in the MS. happened to be blacker than ordinary, which has often been a cause of mistake, it might then have been easily taken for the under-stroke of the mem, and thus give rise to a corrupt reading; add to this, the root כרה carah signifies as well to prepare, as to open, bore, etc. On this supposition the ancient copy translated by the Septuagint, and followed by the apostle, must have read the text thus: אז גוה כרית לי az gevah charitha lli; Σωμα δε κατηρτισω μοι· Then a body thou hast prepared me: thus the Hebrew text, the version of the Septuagint, and the apostle, will agree in what is known to be an indisputable fact in Christianity; namely, that Christ was incarnated for the sin of the world. <div eID="gen19918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19919" type="x-p"/> The Ethiopic has nearly the same reading: the Arabic has both, "A body hast thou prepared me, and mine ears thou hast opened." But the Syriac, the Chaldee, and the Vulgate, agree with the present Hebrew text; and none of the MSS. collated by Kennicott and De Rossi have any various reading on the disputed words. <div eID="gen19919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19920" type="x-p"/> It is remarkable, that all the offerings and sacrifices which were considered to be of an atoning or cleansing nature, offered under the law, are here enumerated by the psalmist and the apostle, to show that none of them, nor all of them, could take away sin; and that the grand sacrifice of Christ was that alone which could do it. <div eID="gen19920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19921" type="x-p"/> Four kinds are here specified, both by the psalmist and the apostle: viz. Sacrifice, זבח zebach, θυσια; Offering, מנחה minchah, προσφορα; Burnt-Offering, עולה olah, ὁλοκαυτωμα; Sin-Offering, חטאה chataah, περι ἁμαρτιας. Of all these we may say, with the apostle, it was impossible that the blood of bulls and goats, etc. should take away sin. <div eID="gen19921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19922" type="x-p"/> Thou hast had no pleasure - Thou couldst never be pleased with the victims under the law; thou couldst never consider them as atonements for sin, as they could never satisfy thy justice, nor make thy law honorable.
entries.e9c990157e2ef6e03e30c098df8ad460093b1f68: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19923" type="x-p"/> In the volume of the book - במגלת ספר bimegillath sepher, "in the roll of the book." Anciently, books were written on skins, and rolled up. Among the Romans, these were called volumina, from volvo, I roll; and the Pentateuch in the Jewish synagogues is still written in this way. There are two wooden rollers; on one they roll on, on the other they roll off, as they proceed in reading. One now lying before me, written on vellum, is two feet two inches in breadth and one hundred and two feet long. To roll and unroll such a MS. was no easy task, and to be managed must lie flat on a table. This contains the Pentateuch only, and is without points, or any other Masoretic distinction. The book mentioned here must be the Pentateuch, or five books of Moses; for, in David's time no other part of Divine revelation had been committed to writing. This whole book speaks about Christ, and his accomplishing the will of God, not only in "the seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent," and "in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed;" but in all the sacrifices and sacrificial rites mentioned in the law.
entries.6148858d7499396719d7e3ba9b9e777a4c1a9762: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19924" type="x-p"/> To do thy will - God willed not the sacrifices under the law, but he willed that a human victim of infinite merit should be offered for the redemption of mankind. That there might be such a victim, a body was prepared for the eternal Logos, and in that body he came to do the will of God; that is, to suffer and die for the sins of the world. <div eID="gen19924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19925" type="x-p"/> 1. Hence we see that the sovereign Will of God is that Jesus should be incarnated; that he should suffer and die; or, in the apostle's words, taste death for every man; that all should believe on him, and be saved from their sins; for this is the Will of God, our sanctification. <div eID="gen19925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19926" type="x-p"/> 2. And as the apostle grounds this on the words of the Psalm, we see that it is the Will of God that that system shall end; for as the essence of it is contained in its sacrifices, and God says he will not have these, and has appointed the Messiah to do his will, i.e., to die for men, hence it necessarily follows, from the psalmist himself, that the introduction of the Messiah into the world is the abolition of the law; and that his sacrifice is that which shall last for ever.
entries.46dd92379a0441735ac1d51fe14ab115b3267d8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19927" type="x-p"/> I have preached righteousness - I think it best to refer these words to Christ and his apostles. In consequence of his having become a sacrifice for sin, the Jewish sacrificial system being ended, the middle wall of partition was broken down, and the door of faith, the doctrine of justification by faith, opened to the Gentiles. Hence the Gospel was preached in all the world, and the mercy of God made known to the Gentiles; and thus righteousness - justification by faith, was preached in the great congregation - to Jews and Gentiles, throughout the Roman empire. <div eID="gen19927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19928" type="x-p"/> The great congregation, both in this and the following verse, I think, means the Gentiles, contradistinguished from the Jews. <div eID="gen19928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19929" type="x-p"/> The word righteousness means the plan or method of salvation by Jesus Christ - God's method of justifying sinners by faith, without the deeds of the law. See <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25-Rom.3.26">Rom 3:25-26</reference> (note), and the notes there.
entries.adc56feb15ace038feddd3b9920e6abd57c86b85: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19930" type="x-p"/> Thy faithfulness - This means the exact fulfillment of the promises made by the prophets relative to the incarnation of Christ, and the opening of the door of faith to the Gentiles. <div eID="gen19930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19931" type="x-p"/> Loving-kindness - Shows the gift itself of Jesus Christ, the highest proof that God could give to a lost world of his mercy, kindness, and loving-kindness.
entries.d2f330fc5eae733a8c59a10c93b44efe0569ae3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19932" type="x-p"/> Thy tender mercies - רחמיך rachameycha, such propensities and feelings as a mother bears to her child; or animals in general to their young. <div eID="gen19932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19933" type="x-p"/> Let thy loving-kindness - חסדך chasdecha, thy overflowing and superabundant mercy. <div eID="gen19933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19934" type="x-p"/> And thy truth - What is revealed in thy word: continually preserve me. Mercy to help me, truth to direct me; and, by the operation of both, I shall be continually preserved from sin and evil.
entries.b60f9905ee7ae9011565763c79f97508e44b59b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19935" type="x-p"/> Innumerable evils have compassed me about - This part does not comport with the preceding; and either argues a former experience, or must be considered a part of another Psalm, written at a different time, and on another occasion, and, were we to prefix the two first verses of the seventieth Psalm to it we should find it to be a Psalm as complete in itself as that is. <div eID="gen19935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19936" type="x-p"/> They are more than the hairs of mine head - This could not be said by any person who was exulting in the pardoning mercy of God, as David was at the time he penned the commencement of this Psalm.
entries.c5e8cc1c557223568cbeeb867fbce69da67e842f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19937" type="x-p"/> That say unto me, Aha, aha - האח האח. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference> (note).
entries.2c4192222f07b94d1b907cf3f314dc2259ff7dd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19938" type="x-p"/> Let all those that seek thee - be glad - In making prayer and supplication to thee, let them ever find thee, that they may magnify thee for the blessings they receive. <div eID="gen19938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19939" type="x-p"/> Love thy salvation - Who earnestly desire to be saved from sin: saved in thy own way, and on thy own terms. <div eID="gen19939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19940" type="x-p"/> The Lord be magnified - Let God be praised continually for the continual blessings he pours down.
entries.5bdaa44d67f8f321c0dad8fb91c0090b59801f3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19941" type="x-p"/> But I am poor - עני ani, afflicted, greatly depressed. <div eID="gen19941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19942" type="x-p"/> And needy - אביון ebyon, a beggar. One utterly destitute, and seeking help. <div eID="gen19942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19943" type="x-p"/> The Lord thinketh upon me - The words are very emphatic; אדני Adonai, my prop, my support, thinketh, יחשב yachshab, meditateth, upon me. On which he concludes: "Thou art my help and deliverer." Seeing that my miserable state occupies thy heart, it will soon employ thy hand. Thou, who meditatest upon me, wilt deliver me. <div eID="gen19943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19944" type="x-p"/> Make no tarrying - Seeing thou art disposed to help, and I am in such great necessity, delay not, but come speedily to my assistance. The old Psalter speaks to this effect: "Let us not be so long under distress and misery that we lose our patience, or our love to thee."  <chapter eID="Ps.40"/> <div eID="gen19944" type="x-p"/>

entries.9ecfd02f53c3a5d4d5a49ebae085ad91c70a8171: <div eID="gen9437" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Thanksgiving, an Offering Up of One’s Self, and Prayer</title> <div sID="gen9438" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.13">Psa 39:1-13</reference> is followed by Psalms 40, because the language of thanksgiving with which it opens is, as it were, the echo of the language of payer contained in the former. If Psalms 40 was composed by David, and not rather by Jeremiah-a question which can only be decided by including Ps 69 (which see) in the same investigation-it belongs to the number of those Psalms which were composed between Gibea of Saul and Ziklag. The mention of the roll of the book in v. 8 harmonizes with the retrospective references to the Tôra, which abound in the Psalms belonging to the time of Saul. And to this we may add the vow to praise Jahve בּקהל, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">Psa 40:10</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.22.26">Psa 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.18">Psa 35:18</reference>; the expression, “more in number than the hairs of my head,” <reference osisRef="Ps.40.13">Psa 40:13</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference>; the wish יצּרוּני, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Psa 25:21</reference>; the mocking האח האה, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.16">Psa 40:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.25">Psa 35:25</reference>; and much besides, on which vid., my <hi type="italic">Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews</hi>, S. 457 transl. vol. ii. p. 149. The second half has an independent form in <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1">Psa 70:1</reference>-5. It is far better adapted to form an independent Psalm than the first half, which merely looks back into the past, and for this very reason contains no prayer. <div eID="gen9438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9439" type="x-p"/> The long lines, more in keeping with the style of prayer than of song, which alternate with disproportionately shorter ones, are characteristic of this Psalm. If with these long lines we associate a few others, which are likewise more or less distinctly indicated, then the Psalm can be easily divided into seven six-line strophes. <div eID="gen9439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9440" type="x-p"/> In the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5-Heb.10.10">Heb 10:5-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference> of this Psalm are, by following the lxx, taken as the language of the Christ at His coming into the world. There can be no doubt in this particular instance that, as we look to the second part of the Psalm, this rendering is brought about typically. The words of David, the anointed one, but only now on the way to the throne, are so moulded by the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of prophecy, that they sound at the same time like the words of the second David, passing through suffering to glory, whose offering up of Himself is the close of the animal sacrifices, and whose person and work are the very kernel and star of the roll of the Law. We are not thereby compelled to understand the whole Psalm as typically predictive. It again descends from the typically prophetic height to which it has risen even from <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">Psa 40:10</reference> onwards; and from <reference osisRef="Ps.40.13">Psa 40:13</reference> onwards, the typically prophetic strain which still lingers in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.10">Psa 40:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.40.11">Psa 40:11</reference> has entirely ceased.
entries.162f78dfb24109595ccd5529b53d9b8077ac1ac2: <reference osisRef="Ps.40.1-Ps.40.4">Psa 40:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9441" type="x-p"/> David, who, though not without some hesitation, we regard as the author, now finds himself in a situation in which, on the one hand, he has just been rescued from danger, and, on the other, is still exposed to peril. Under such circumstances praise rightly occupies the first place, as in general, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Psa 50:23</reference>, gratitude is the way to salvation. His hope, although תּוחלת ממשּׁכה (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.12">Pro 13:12</reference>), has not deceived him; he is rescued, and can now again sing a new song of thanksgiving, an example for others, strengthening their trust. קוּה קוּיתי, I waited with constancy and perseverance. יהוה is the accusative as in <reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.5">Psa 130:5</reference>, and not the vocative as in Psa 39:8. אזנו is to be supplied in thought to ויּט, although after the analogy of <reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">Psa 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.3">Psa 31:3</reference>, one might have looked for the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. wayaT instead of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>. בור שׁאון does not mean a pit of roaring (of water), since שׁאון standing alone (see, on the other hand, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.8">Psa 65:8</reference>, Isa 17:12.) has not this meaning; and, moreover, “rushing, roaring” (Hengstenberg), tumultuous waters of a pit or a cistern does not furnish any idea that is true to nature; neither does it mean a pit of falling in, since שׁאה does not exhibit the signification <hi type="italic">deorsum</hi> <hi type="italic">labi</hi>; but the meaning is: a pit of devastation, of destruction, of ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.31">Jer 25:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.17">Jer 46:17</reference>), vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi> on Psa 35:8. Another figure is “mire of the marsh” (יון found only here and in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">Psa 69:3</reference>), i.e., water, in the miry bottom of which one can find no firm footing - a combination like מטר־גּשׁם, Zec 10:1, אדמת־עפר, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan 12:2</reference>, explained in the Mishna, <hi type="italic">Mikvaoth</hi> ix. 2, by טיט הבורות (mire of the cisterns). Taking them out of this, Jahve placed his feet upon a rock, established his footsteps, i.e., removed him from the danger which surrounded him, and gave him firm ground under his feet. The high rock and the firm footsteps are the opposites of the deep pit and the yielding miry bottom. This deliverance afforded him new matter for thanksgiving (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.33.3">Psa 33:3</reference>), and became in his mouth “praise to our God;” for the deliverance of the chosen king is an act of the God of Israel on behalf of His chosen people. The futures in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference> </hi>(with an alliteration similar to <reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Psa 52:8</reference>) indicate, by their being thus cumulative, that they are intended of the present and of that which still continues in the future.
entries.99d170bd8595934066077645b9808638a3eaed85: <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5-Ps.40.6">Psa 40:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen9441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9442" type="x-p"/> He esteems him happy who puts his trust (מבטחו, with a latent <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, as, according to Kimchi, also in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.5">Psa 71:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.24">Job 31:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.7">Jer 17:7</reference>) in Jahve, the God who has already made Himself glorious in Israel by innumerable wonderful works. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.7">Jer 17:7</reference> is an echo of this אשׁרי. <reference osisRef="Ps.52.9">Psa 52:9</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.91.9">Psa 91:9</reference>) shows how Davidic is the language. The expression is designedly not האישׁ, but הגּבר, which is better adapted to designate the man as being tempted to put trust in himself. רהבים from רהב (not from רהב) are the impetuous or violent, who in their arrogance cast down everything.  שׂטי כזב, “turners aside of falsehood” (שׁוּט = שׂטה, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">Psa 101:3</reference>), is the expression for apostates who yield to falsehood instead of to the truth: to take כּזב as accusative of the aim is forbidden by the <hi type="italic">status construct</hi>.; to take it as the genitive in the sense of the accusative of the object (like תם הלכי, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>) is impracticable, because שׂוט (שׂטה) does not admit of a transitive sense; כזב is, therefore, <hi type="italic">genit. qualit.</hi> like און in Psa 59:6. This second strophe contains two practical applications of that which the writer himself has experienced. From this point of view, he who trusts in God appears to the poet to be supremely happy, and a distant view of God’s gracious rule over His own people opens up before him. נפלאות are the thoughts of God realized, and מחשׁבות those that are being realized, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.29">Jer 51:29</reference>; Isa 55:8. רבּות is an accusative of the predicate: in great number, in rich abundance; אלינוּ, “for us,” as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">Jer 15:1</reference> (Ew. §217, c). His doings towards Israel were from of old a fulness of wondrous deeds and plans of deliverance, which was ever realizing and revealing itself. There is not ערך אליך, a possibility of comparison with Thee, οὐκ ἔστι (Ew. §§321, <hi type="italic">c</hi>) ἰσουν τί σοι - ערך as in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.7">Psa 89:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.18">Isa 40:18</reference> - they are too powerful (עצם of a powerful sum, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.5.6">Jer 5:6</reference>) for one to enumerate. According to Rosenmüller, Stier, and Hupfeld, אין ערך אליך even affirms the same thing in other words: it is not possible to lay them forth to Thee (before Thee); but that man should “lay forth” (Symmachus ἐκθέστηαι) before God His marvellous works and His thoughts of salvation, is an unbecoming conception. The cohortative forms, which follow, אגּידה ואדבּרה ,wollof h, admit of being taken as a protasis to what follows, after the analogy of <reference osisRef="Job.19.18">Job 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.6">Job 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.26">Job 30:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference> : if I wish to declare them and speak them forth, they are too powerful (numerous) to be enumerated (Ges. §128, 1, <hi type="italic">d</hi>). The accentuation, however, renders it as a parenthetical clause: I would (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.18">Psa 51:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.13">Psa 55:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.10">Psa 6:10</reference>) declare them and speak them forth. He would do this, but because God, in the fulness of His wondrous works and thoughts of salvation, is absolutely without an equal, he is obliged to leave it undone - they are so powerful (numerous) that the enumeration of them falls far short of their powerful fulness. The words <hi type="italic">alioqui pronunciarem et eloquerer</hi> have the character of a parenthesis, and, as <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference> shows, this accords with the style of this Psalm.
entries.97660ee3cfec1393148c2dffceaac784a0d02dd3: <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7-Ps.40.9">Psa 40:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen9442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9443" type="x-p"/> The connection of the thoughts is clear: great and manifold are the proofs of Thy loving-kindness, how am I to render thanks to Thee for them? To this question he first of all gives a negative answer: God delights not in outward sacrifices. The sacrifices are named in a twofold way: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) according to the material of which they consist, viz., זבח, the animal sacrifice, and מנחה, the meal or meat offering (including the נסך, the wine or drink offering, which is the inalienable accessory of the accompanying <hi type="italic">mincha</hi>); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) according to their purpose, in accordance with which they bring about either the turning towards one of the good pleasure of God, as more especially in the case of the עולה, or, as more especially in the case of the הטּאת (in this passage חטאה), the turning away of the divine displeasure. The fact of the זבח and עולה standing first, has, moreover, its special reason in the fact that זבח specially designates the <hi type="italic">shelamı̂m</hi> offerings, and to the province of these latter belongs the thank-offering proper, viz., the <hi type="italic">tôda - shelamı̂m</hi> offering; and that עולה as the sacrifice of adoration (προσευχή), which is also always a general thanksgiving (εὐχαριστία), is most natural, side by side with the shalemim, to him who gives thanks. When it is said of God, that He does not delight in and desire such non-personal sacrifices, there is as little intention as in <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22">Jer 7:22</reference> (cf. Amo 5:21.) of saying that the sacrificial Tôra is not of divine origin, but that the true, essential will of God is not directed to such sacrifices. <div eID="gen9443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9444" type="x-p"/> Between these synonymous utterances in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference> </hi>and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference></hi> stands the clause אזנים כּרית לּי. In connection with this position it is natural, with Rosenmüller, Gesenius, De Wette, and Stier, to explain it “ears hast Thou pierced for me” = this hast Thou engraven upon my mind as a revelation, this disclosure hast Thou imparted to me. But, although כּרה, to dig, is even admissible in the sense of digging through, piercing (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.22.17">Psa 22:17</reference>), there are two considerations against this interpretation, viz.: (1) that then one would rather look for אזן instead of אזנים after the analogy of the phrases גּלה אזן, חעיר אזן, and פּתח אזן, since the inner sense, in which the external organs of sense, with their functions, have their basis of unity, is commonly denoted by the use of the singular; (2) that according to the syntax, חפצתּ, כּרית, and שׁאלתּ are all placed on the same level. Thus, therefore, it is with this very אזנים כרית לי that the answer is intended, in its positive form, to begin; and the primary passage, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>, favours this view: <hi type="italic">“Hath Jahve delight in whole burnt-offerings and sacrifices as in one’s obeying the voice of Jahve? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, to attend better than the fat of rams!”</hi> The assertion of David is the echo of this assertion of Samuel, by which the sentence of death was pronounced upon the kingship of Saul, and consequently the way of that which is well-pleasing to God was traced out for the future kingship of David. God - says David - desires not outward sacrifices, but obedience; ears hath He digged for me, i.e., formed the sense of hearing, bestowed the faculty of hearing, and given therewith the instruction to obey.<note placement="foot">There is a similar expression in the Tamul Kural, Graul’s translation, S. 63, No. 418: “An ear, that was not hollowed out by hearing, has, even if hearing, the manner of not hearing.” The “hollowing out” meaning in this passage an opening of the inward sense of hearing by instruction.</note> <div eID="gen9444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9445" type="x-p"/> The idea is not that God has given him ears in order to hear that disclosure concerning the true will of God (Hupfeld), but, in general, to hear the word of God, and to obey that which is heard. God desires not sacrifices but hearing ears, and consequently the submission of the person himself in willing obedience. To interpret it “Thou hast appropriated me to Thyself לעבד עולם,” after <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.15.17">Deu 15:17</reference>, would not be out of harmony with the context; but it is at once shut out by the fact that the word is not אזן, but אזנים.
